title: Travel Problems
subtitle: Handle delays, emergencies, and disasters like a seasoned traveller

lessons.title: Retards et annulations
lessons.description: Complain politely about delays and cancellations, and understand what airlines and railways owe you.

blocks.heading: When things go wrong at the station or airport
blocks.body: Travel rarely goes exactly to plan. Trains run "en retard" (late), flights get "annulés" (cancelled), and strikes ("grèves") can throw an entire trip into chaos. B1 French gives you the vocabulary to describe exactly what happened and to stay calm while doing it.

examples.french: Mon train a du retard.
examples.english: My train is late.

examples.french: Le vol est annulé à cause d'une grève.
examples.english: The flight is cancelled because of a strike.

examples.french: Nous avons raté notre correspondance.
examples.english: We missed our connection.

examples.french: Il y a eu une panne sur la ligne.
examples.english: There was a breakdown on the line.

examples.french: On nous a proposé un vol de remplacement.
examples.english: We were offered a replacement flight.

blocks.tip: "En retard" describes a person or vehicle that is late; "retardé(e)" describes something that has been delayed by an external cause.

blocks.heading: Complaining without losing your cool
blocks.body: French customer-service culture rewards politeness even when you're frustrated. Soften a complaint with the conditional ("je voudrais", "j'aimerais", "pourriez-vous") and be specific about what you're asking for — a refund, a voucher, or compensation.

examples.french: Je voudrais me plaindre du service.
examples.english: I would like to complain about the service.

examples.french: Pourriez-vous me rembourser mon billet ?
examples.english: Could you refund my ticket?

examples.french: J'aimerais un dédommagement pour ce retard.
examples.english: I would like compensation for this delay.

examples.french: Nous avons droit à un remboursement, je crois.
examples.english: We're entitled to a refund, I believe.

examples.french: C'est la deuxième fois que ça arrive, franchement.
examples.english: It's the second time this has happened, honestly.

blocks.tip: Starting with "je comprends que..." before your complaint ("I understand that...") tends to get a friendlier response from staff.

blocks.heading: Asking for what you're owed
blocks.body: European rules give travellers real rights when flights are delayed or cancelled: a free meal, a hotel room, or a cash refund, depending on how long the delay is. Knowing the right words helps you ask for them clearly at the "guichet" (counter).

examples.english: This ticket is valid for another train today.

examples.english: The airline must give you a meal voucher.

blocks.heading: The conditional for polite requests
blocks.body: The conditional ("je voudrais", "j'aimerais", "pourriez-vous") softens a demand into a polite request — essential when you're annoyed but still need someone's help. Form it with the future stem + imperfect endings: "je voudrais", "nous aimerions", "pourriez-vous".

examples.french: Je voudrais un remboursement, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: I would like a refund, please.

examples.french: Pourriez-vous vérifier l'horaire du prochain train ?
examples.english: Could you check the schedule for the next train?

examples.french: J'aimerais parler à un responsable.
examples.english: I would like to speak to a manager.

examples.french: Nous voudrions un geste commercial pour ce désagrément.
examples.english: We would like a goodwill gesture for this inconvenience.

examples.french: Sauriez-vous à quelle heure part le bus de remplacement ?
examples.english: Would you happen to know what time the replacement bus leaves?

blocks.tip: Compare "je veux" (I want, blunt) with "je voudrais" (I would like, polite) — the second is far more common in real complaints.

blocks.heading: Relative pronouns qui, que, dont
blocks.body: Relative pronouns let you pack more information into one sentence when describing a problem. "Qui" replaces a subject, "que" replaces a direct object, and "dont" replaces something introduced by "de" (like "se plaindre de" or "avoir besoin de").

examples.french: Le train qui devait partir à huit heures a du retard.
examples.english: The train that was supposed to leave at eight is late.

examples.french: C'est le vol que nous avons raté.
examples.english: That's the flight that we missed.

examples.french: La compagnie dont je me plains n'a pas répondu.
examples.english: The company I'm complaining about hasn't replied.

examples.french: Voici le billet dont j'ai besoin pour le remboursement.
examples.english: Here is the ticket I need for the refund.

examples.french: L'agent qui m'a répondu était très patient.
examples.english: The agent who answered me was very patient.

blocks.tip: A quick test: if the missing word would need "de" in front of it, use "dont" — never "que" or "qui".

passages.title: Un mail au service client
passages.french:
Madame, Monsieur,
Je vous écris au sujet de mon vol Paris-Marseille du 3 août, qui a été annulé sans aucune explication.
J'ai attendu trois heures au guichet avant qu'un agent ne m'informe de l'annulation.
On m'a proposé un vol de remplacement le lendemain, mais personne ne m'a parlé d'hébergement pour la nuit.
J'ai donc dû réserver un hôtel à mes frais, alors que la loi européenne prévoit un logement gratuit dans ce genre de situation.
De plus, j'ai raté un rendez-vous professionnel important à cause de ce retard, ce qui m'a causé un vrai préjudice.
Mes collègues ont dû se débrouiller sans moi pendant toute la matinée.
Je voudrais donc obtenir le remboursement de mon billet ainsi qu'un dédommagement pour ce désagrément.
J'espère une réponse rapide et un geste commercial de votre part.
Je vous remercie par avance de l'attention que vous porterez à ma réclamation.
Cordialement,
Sophie Marchand
passages.english:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to you about my Paris-Marseille flight on August 3rd, which was cancelled without any explanation.
I waited three hours at the counter before an agent informed me of the cancellation.
I was offered a replacement flight the next day, but no one told me about accommodation for the night.
So I had to book a hotel at my own expense, even though European law provides for free accommodation in this kind of situation.
Moreover, I missed an important work appointment because of this delay, which caused me real harm.
My colleagues had to manage without me for the whole morning.
I would therefore like to obtain a refund for my ticket as well as compensation for this inconvenience.
I hope for a prompt reply and a goodwill gesture from you.
Thank you in advance for the attention you will give to my complaint.
Regards,
Sophie Marchand

lessons.title: Perdu à l'étranger
lessons.description: Handle emergencies abroad: lost documents, theft, and calling the right people for help.

blocks.heading: Lost documents, lost calm
blocks.body: Losing a passport or wallet abroad is stressful, but a clear sentence structure helps: describe what happened, what you lost, and what you need. "Je me suis fait voler..." (I had ... stolen) is the go-to construction for reporting theft.

examples.french: J'ai perdu mon passeport.
examples.english: I lost my passport.

examples.french: On m'a volé mon sac.
examples.english: Someone stole my bag.

examples.french: Je me suis fait voler ma carte bancaire.
examples.english: I had my bank card stolen.

examples.french: Je suis perdu, vous pouvez m'aider ?
examples.english: I'm lost, can you help me?

examples.french: Mes papiers sont égarés depuis ce matin.
examples.english: My papers have been missing since this morning.

blocks.tip: "Je me suis fait voler" literally means "I made myself get stolen from" — it's the natural French way to say something was stolen from you.

blocks.heading: Who to call
blocks.body: Different problems need different institutions: the "commissariat" (police station) for theft, the "ambassade" or "consulat" for a lost passport, and the emergency number for a medical problem. Knowing which to call saves precious time.

examples.french: Il faut porter plainte au commissariat.
examples.english: You need to file a complaint at the police station.

examples.french: L'ambassade peut délivrer un passeport provisoire.
examples.english: The embassy can issue a temporary passport.

examples.french: En cas d'urgence, appelez le cent douze.
examples.english: In an emergency, call 112.

examples.french: J'ai fait opposition à ma carte bancaire tout de suite.
examples.english: I blocked my bank card straight away.

examples.french: L'assurance voyage couvre le vol de bagages.
examples.english: Travel insurance covers luggage theft.

blocks.tip: 112 works as a free emergency number anywhere in the European Union, not just in France.

blocks.heading: Asking for help clearly
blocks.body: When you're stressed, short, direct sentences work best. Use "il faut que" + subjunctive to express urgency, and don't hesitate to ask someone to slow down or repeat: "vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?"

examples.english: I need to go to the hospital.

examples.french: Il faut que vous m'aidiez, c'est urgent.
examples.english: You need to help me, it's urgent.

blocks.heading: Reflexive verbs in the passé composé
blocks.body: Reflexive verbs like "se perdre" (to get lost) and "se faire voler" (to get robbed) use "être" in the passé composé, and the past participle agrees with the subject. This construction is essential for narrating what happened to you.

examples.french: Je me suis perdu(e) dans la vieille ville.
examples.english: I got lost in the old town.

examples.french: Elle s'est fait voler son passeport.
examples.english: She had her passport stolen.

examples.french: Nous nous sommes trompés de rue.
examples.english: We took the wrong street.

examples.french: Ils se sont fait aider par la police locale.
examples.english: They got help from the local police.

examples.french: Vous vous êtes bien débrouillé, malgré la panique.
examples.english: You managed well, despite the panic.

blocks.tip: "Se faire" + infinitive describes something happening TO you (often unwelcome) — very different from a plain reflexive action.

blocks.heading: Il faut que + subjunctive for urgency
blocks.body: "Il faut que" expresses necessity and is always followed by the subjunctive. In an emergency, it's the fastest way to say what absolutely must happen.

examples.french: Il faut que j'appelle l'ambassade.
examples.english: I need to call the embassy.

examples.french: Il faut que vous fassiez une déclaration de perte.
examples.english: You need to file a loss report.

examples.french: Il faut qu'on aille au commissariat maintenant.
examples.english: We need to go to the police station now.

examples.french: Il faut que je sois calme pour expliquer la situation.
examples.english: I need to stay calm to explain the situation.

examples.french: Il ne faut pas que tu perdes tes papiers d'identité.
examples.english: You must not lose your ID papers.

blocks.tip: Common irregular subjunctives to know here: "aller" → "que j'aille", "faire" → "que je fasse", "être" → "que je sois".

items.tip: The impersonal "on" is common when the thief is unknown — no need to say "quelqu'un".

items.english: I need to go to the police station to file a report.
items.tip: Remember "aille" is the irregular subjunctive of "aller" — it doesn't sound like the present tense "vais".

items.tip: "Y a-t-il" is a formal, written-sounding way of asking "is there" — useful in official settings like an embassy.

passages.title: Une mauvaise surprise à Lisbonne
passages.french:
Léa voyageait seule au Portugal quand elle s'est rendu compte, en sortant du tram, que son sac avait disparu.
À l'intérieur : son passeport, sa carte bancaire et tout son argent liquide.
Elle a d'abord paniqué, puis elle s'est souvenue des conseils de son père : rester calme et agir dans l'ordre.
Elle a d'abord téléphoné à sa banque pour faire opposition à sa carte, avant même de chercher son sac.
Ensuite, elle s'est rendue au commissariat le plus proche pour porter plainte.
L'agent lui a remis une déclaration de vol, nécessaire pour l'assurance voyage.
Elle a aussi appelé ses parents pour les rassurer, même si elle avait encore un peu peur.
Le lendemain matin, elle a appelé le consulat de France pour demander un passeport provisoire.
Une employée très patiente l'a rassurée : "Ce genre de situation arrive souvent, on va vous aider."
Un interprète était même disponible pour l'aider à remplir les formulaires.
Grâce à cette aide, Léa a pu reprendre son voyage dès le surlendemain.
Elle voyage aujourd'hui un peu plus prudente qu'avant.
passages.english:
Léa was travelling alone in Portugal when she realised, getting off the tram, that her bag had disappeared.
Inside: her passport, her bank card and all her cash.
She panicked at first, then remembered her father's advice: stay calm and act in order.
She first phoned her bank to block her card, even before looking for her bag.
Then she went to the nearest police station to file a report.
The officer gave her a theft declaration, needed for travel insurance.
She also called her parents to reassure them, even though she was still a little scared.
The next morning, she called the French consulate to ask for a temporary passport.
A very patient employee reassured her: "This kind of situation happens often, we'll help you."
An interpreter was even available to help her fill in the forms.
Thanks to this help, Léa was able to resume her trip the day after next.
She travels today a little more carefully than before.

lessons.title: Raconter un voyage raté
lessons.description: Tell the story of a trip that went hilariously wrong, mixing imparfait and passé composé.

blocks.heading: Setting the scene vs. the events
blocks.body: Good storytelling mixes two past tenses: the "imparfait" paints the background (what things were like), and the "passé composé" marks the events (what happened, one after another). This contrast is what makes a travel disaster story fun to tell.

examples.french: Il pleuvait quand nous sommes arrivés à l'hôtel.
examples.english: It was raining when we arrived at the hotel.

examples.french: Nous étions fatigués, et soudain le train est parti sans nous.
examples.english: We were tired, and suddenly the train left without us.

examples.french: J'étais persuadé d'avoir réservé le bon hôtel.
examples.english: I was convinced I had booked the right hotel.

examples.french: Tout allait bien jusqu'à ce que nous perdions les billets.
examples.english: Everything was going fine until we lost the tickets.

examples.french: Le voyage a viré à la catastrophe en une heure.
examples.english: The trip turned into a disaster within an hour.

blocks.tip: If you can rephrase it as "was/were -ing" or "used to", it's imparfait; if it's a one-off completed action, use passé composé.

blocks.heading: Building suspense and comedy
blocks.body: Connectors like "soudain", "tout à coup" and "du coup" build tension and humour into a story. French speakers love the self-deprecating twist: describing something going wrong, then laughing about it with "heureusement" or "avec le recul" (looking back).

examples.french: Tout à coup, la pluie s'est transformée en orage.
examples.english: Suddenly, the rain turned into a storm.

examples.french: Du coup, on a dormi dans le hall de la gare.
examples.english: So we ended up sleeping in the station hall.

examples.french: Avec le recul, c'est plutôt drôle.
examples.english: Looking back, it's actually pretty funny.

examples.french: Franchement, on a eu un fou rire dans le taxi.
examples.english: Honestly, we had a fit of laughter in the taxi.

examples.french: Bref, ce voyage restera inoubliable.
examples.english: In short, this trip will remain unforgettable.

blocks.tip: "Du coup" is very common in spoken French to mean "so / as a result" — perfect for chaining one mishap to the next.

blocks.heading: Turning disaster into a good story
blocks.body: The best travel stories admit things went wrong before finding the silver lining. Use "pas de chance" (bad luck) for the low point, and "par miracle" or "finalement" to mark the turnaround.

examples.french: Pas de chance, notre hôtel avait fermé pour travaux.
examples.english: Bad luck, our hotel had closed for renovations.

examples.french: Par miracle, un voisin nous a proposé son canapé.
examples.english: Miraculously, a neighbour offered us their sofa.

examples.french: Ce voyage raté est devenu ma meilleure anecdote.
examples.english: This failed trip became my best anecdote.

examples.french: On a fini par en rire, tellement c'était absurde.
examples.english: We ended up laughing about it, it was so absurd.

blocks.heading: Imparfait vs. passé composé, side by side
blocks.body: In a single story, both tenses usually appear together: the imparfait describes the ongoing situation, and the passé composé interrupts it with a sudden event. Notice how French marks that interruption with words like "quand" and "soudain".

examples.french: On dormait quand le réveil de l'hôtel a sonné une heure trop tôt.
examples.english: We were sleeping when the hotel alarm rang an hour too early.

examples.french: Il faisait nuit noire quand nous sommes arrivés au camping.
examples.english: It was pitch dark when we arrived at the campsite.

examples.french: Je pensais avoir tout prévu, et puis j'ai perdu les billets.
examples.english: I thought I had planned everything, and then I lost the tickets.

examples.french: Tout semblait normal jusqu'à ce que le bus tombe en panne.
examples.english: Everything seemed normal until the bus broke down.

examples.french: Nous étions au milieu du pont quand il a commencé à pleuvoir.
examples.english: We were in the middle of the bridge when it started to rain.

blocks.tip: A simple rule: the imparfait sets the stage, the passé composé moves the plot forward.

blocks.heading: The plus-que-parfait for "had already happened"
blocks.body: To explain that something had already happened before the main story event, use the plus-que-parfait ("avais/étais" + past participle). It's the tense of hindsight and excuses — perfect for a comically unlucky travel story.

examples.french: Le train était déjà parti quand nous sommes arrivés.
examples.english: The train had already left when we arrived.

examples.french: J'avais oublié mon passeport à la maison.
examples.english: I had forgotten my passport at home.

examples.french: Nous n'avions pas réservé, et l'hôtel était complet.
examples.english: We hadn't booked, and the hotel was full.

examples.french: Elle avait perdu son billet avant même d'arriver à la gare.
examples.english: She had lost her ticket even before reaching the station.

examples.french: On s'était trompés de jour pour toute la réservation.
examples.english: We had got the wrong day for the entire booking.

blocks.tip: Form it like the passé composé, but put "avoir" or "être" in the imparfait: "j'avais fait", "j'étais parti(e)".

passages.title: Le pire week-end de ma vie (ou presque)
passages.french:
On voulait passer un week-end tranquille à Nice.
Décidément, rien ne s'est passé comme prévu.
D'abord, on s'est trompés de gare : on est allés à Nice-Ville alors que notre train partait de Nice-Saint-Augustin.
Du coup, on a raté notre train de dix minutes.
Ensuite, en achetant de nouveaux billets, j'ai réalisé que j'avais laissé mon portefeuille dans le premier train.
Pas de chance.
Heureusement, une contrôleuse très gentille l'avait retrouvé et me l'a rapporté avant le départ.
Arrivés enfin à l'hôtel, on a découvert que ma sœur avait réservé la mauvaise date : notre chambre était déjà occupée !
Franchement, on ne savait plus si on devait rire ou pleurer.
Par miracle, l'hôtel d'à côté avait justement une chambre libre.
On y a passé une nuit bien plus confortable que prévu, en racontant déjà l'histoire en riant.
Bref, ce voyage raté est devenu, avec le recul, notre meilleure anecdote de famille.
On en rigole encore à chaque repas de Noël.
passages.english:
We wanted to spend a quiet weekend in Nice.
Decidedly, nothing went as planned.
First, we went to the wrong station: we went to Nice-Ville when our train left from Nice-Saint-Augustin.
So we missed our train by ten minutes.
Then, while buying new tickets, I realised I had left my wallet on the first train.
Bad luck.
Fortunately, a very kind ticket inspector had found it and brought it back to me before departure.
Having finally arrived at the hotel, we discovered that my sister had booked the wrong date: our room was already occupied!
Honestly, we didn't know whether to laugh or cry anymore.
Miraculously, the hotel next door happened to have a free room.
We spent a much comfier night than expected there, already telling the story with laughter.
In short, this failed trip became, looking back, our best family anecdote.
We still laugh about it at every Christmas dinner.
